title: We Drained the Edmund Fitzgerald's Graveyard. Here's What Was Hidden.
voice: Use the same voice as videos 1 to 4 (Sawyer, Midnight Storyteller) with exactly the same settings, so the channel always sounds like one narrator.

sections.title: Seventeen miles
sections.dir: Quiet and gripping, like the start of a true mystery. Say "Seventeen miles." slowly, as its own sentence. Pause after each item in the fourth paragraph. "So let's drain it." is said plainly. The last paragraph is warmer and direct.
paras: Seventeen miles. That's how far the Edmund Fitzgerald was from safety when she disappeared. Seventeen miles from Whitefish Point, and the shelter of the bay behind it. At full speed, just over an hour.
At ten past seven, her captain radioed the ship behind him. "We are holding our own."
Minutes later, she was gone. Twenty-nine men.

She went down at the edge of the most dangerous water on Lake Superior. Sailors call it the Graveyard of the Great Lakes. It has taken at least two hundred and forty ships. A steamer carrying seventy tons of silver ore that has never been accounted for. A freighter that exploded when the cold water reached her boilers. A captain who survived twenty hours clinging to the roof of his pilothouse. And almost all of them are still down there.
So let's drain it.

We can't really, of course. But divers, sonar and two hundred years of shipwreck records have shown us what's down there. So we're going to lower the water, a few feet at a time, and watch the graveyard appear.

And watch for this. Every ship down there was killed by something. By the time we reach the bottom, five hundred and thirty feet down, you'll see that on the night the Fitzgerald sank, every one of those killers was waiting for her.

This is Great Lakes Files. We go looking for the places hidden in and under these lakes. A lot of you found us through our last Edmund Fitzgerald video, so welcome. Most people watching haven't subscribed yet. If you like this kind of story, tap subscribe right now. It's free, it takes one second, and it's what keeps this channel going.

sections.title: Three killers
sections.dir: Steady and vivid. Slow down for "Three things kill them here." A short pause after "The storm.", "The dark." and "And the cold." "Let's start the drain." is said plainly, with a small pause before it.
paras: The point is called Whitefish Point, at the eastern end of Lake Superior. Every ship entering or leaving the lake has to pass it, and more ships have been lost around it than anywhere else on Lake Superior.
Three things kill them here.
The storm. Behind the point lie a hundred and sixty miles of open water, so a gale from the northwest has room to build waves of thirty feet or more.
The dark. Night, fog, snow squalls, even the smoke of forest fires, in a lane crowded with ships.
And the cold. Lake Superior is so cold that, as sailors say, she seldom gives up her dead.
Remember those three. The storm, the dark, and the cold. Let's start the drain.

sections.title: Twenty feet
sections.dir: Brisk and vivid, like a countdown. A short pause after each depth ("Twenty feet." "Thirty feet.") and after "The storm." The last line drops lower, with suspense.
paras: Twenty feet. Just west of the lighthouse, which has stood on the point since eighteen forty-nine, the bottom starts to show, and the first wreck appears, in pieces. The schooner barge Saturn. In November, eighteen seventy-two, an arctic gale snapped the towline between her and the steamer pulling her. She was driven onto the bottom here and pounded apart. Seven men died. The storm.

Thirty feet. To the west, the wreck of the schooner Allegheny comes out of the water. She was stranded in a gale in nineteen thirteen, and the lifesaving crew from Vermilion Point got every man off alive.
Not every crew here was that lucky.

sections.title: Fifty feet
sections.dir: Storytelling, building tension. Slow and steady through the rescue attempts. A real pause after "She sank in four minutes." and after "He was the only survivor." Respectful, never dramatic, for the paragraph about the crew.
paras: At fifty feet, a mile and a half from the point, a wooden steamer appears. Her name is the Myron.

On the twenty-second of November, nineteen nineteen, she left Munising piled high with lumber, towing a barge called the Miztec. Two hours later, a November gale hit them, with winds of sixty miles an hour, heavy snow, and the temperature falling fast. The seas opened the seams of her old wooden hull. Ice built up on her until she could barely make headway.

Her captain left the barge at anchor to ride out the storm, and fought on toward the shelter of Whitefish Bay. A bigger steel steamer ran alongside to shield her from the waves. A lifesaving crew followed in a small boat.
A mile and a half from the point... the water reached her boiler fires. She sank in four minutes.

Her crew got into the lifeboats, but they were trapped in a sea of floating lumber. Two steamers tried to reach them. One got close enough to throw them lines, but their hands were too frozen to hold on.

Her captain was still inside the pilothouse when it tore away from the ship. He climbed out through the window and held on to the roof. Twenty hours later, a steamer coming up from the Soo found him, still on that roof, drifting miles away, his clothes frozen to his body. He was the only survivor.

Remember what sailors say about Lake Superior and her dead? This time, the lake gave up every one. All seventeen men were found, still in their life jackets, covered in ice. Some were found days later, in a lifeboat. Eight weren't found until the next spring, frozen into the ice along the shore. People from the towns around the bay cut them free and buried them in a small cemetery called Mission Hill.

And the barge the Myron left at anchor, the Miztec? She rode out that storm. Two years later, she sank off the same shore with all seven of her crew. Today she lies a few miles from the Myron, at the same depth.

sections.title: A hundred feet
sections.dir: Calmer, with a sense of wonder for the museum paragraph. Then direct and friendly for the guess, like talking to one person. The last line has a little suspense.
paras: A hundred feet. Seven miles out from the lighthouse, the schooner barge Niagara appears. In September, eighteen eighty-seven, she broke loose from the steamer towing her and went down. All nine people on board were lost.

At a hundred and twenty feet, there's a steamer called the Vienna. She sank in eighteen seventy-three after a collision, and everyone aboard got off alive. In this graveyard, that makes her one of the lucky ones.

The water here is cold and clear, and wrecks last a long time in it. This is one of the last places in the Great Lakes where the wrecks aren't covered in zebra mussels. Three hundred and seventy-six square miles of it are now a protected preserve, and divers call it an underwater museum.

We're about halfway down. So before we go deeper, take a guess. What do you think really sank the Edmund Fitzgerald? The storm? The hatch covers? A shoal? Or something wrong with the ship herself? Put your guess in the comments right now. One word is enough. Then, at the end, see if you've changed your mind.
And stay with me, because below this, the wrecks get bigger, and the dark becomes the killer.

sections.title: Two hundred feet
sections.dir: Storytelling with a spark of treasure-hunt intrigue. Slow down for "seventy tons of silver ore from Montana." and for the last sentence.
paras: As the water falls toward two hundred feet, a steel freighter appears, the John B. Cowle. In July, nineteen-oh-nine, she collided with another freighter right here in Whitefish Bay and sank. Fourteen of her twenty-four crew died.
And then, at two hundred feet, the wreck treasure hunters have talked about for a century and a half. The Comet.

On a clear, starlit night in August, eighteen seventy-five, she rounded the Whitefish Point light, heading for the Soo. In the dusk, her lookout saw a steamer's lights ahead. Her captain turned to avoid them, and found himself crossing right in front of the other ship. The Canadian steamer Manitoba struck her and cut deep into her side. A witness said her upper decks crumbled and sank in about a minute. Ten men died.

In her hold were five hundred tons of pig iron, some copper, and seventy tons of silver ore from Montana. People tried to salvage it in eighteen seventy-six, and again in nineteen thirty-eight. Both times, they couldn't even find the wreck. Divers finally found her in the nineteen seventies. But what happened to the silver ore is still unknown.

sections.title: Two hundred and seventy feet
sections.dir: Serious and vivid. Read the explosion simply, without drama. A real pause after "Twenty-nine people died." and before "Twenty-nine." at the end.
paras: Below two hundred feet, the bottom of the bay falls away. And at the deepest point of the preserve, about two hundred and seventy feet down, lies the Superior City.
When she was launched in eighteen ninety-eight, she was the largest ship ever built on fresh water. The whole town of Lorain, Ohio, crowded the riverbank to watch.

At ten past nine on the night of the twentieth of August, nineteen twenty, she was heading down into Whitefish Bay with seven thousand six hundred tons of iron ore. In the dark, another freighter, the Willis L. King, was coming the other way. The King hit her in the side.
Cold lake water rushed in and reached her boilers. They exploded, and her stern was nearly blown off. Most of the crew had run to the lifeboats, which hung right above the boilers.
Twenty-nine people died. Twenty-eight men and one woman. Only four survived. One of them was blown straight off the ship by the explosion, and was found floating on a hatch cover.
It was the worst collision in the history of Lake Superior. The dark, and the cold. Remember that number... Twenty-nine.

sections.title: Five hundred and thirty feet
sections.dir: Slow, quiet and respectful. A real pause before "The Edmund Fitzgerald." A short pause after "The storm.", "The dark." and "And the cold." Read the captain's words plainly. The last paragraph is direct and warm.
paras: Now the water keeps falling, past the preserve, past the mouth of the bay, and out into open Lake Superior. Seventeen miles from Whitefish Point, just across the border in Canadian waters, five hundred and thirty feet down... she appears.
The Edmund Fitzgerald.
Seven hundred and twenty-nine feet long, the largest ship ever to sink on the Great Lakes. And on her last night, all three of this graveyard's killers were waiting for her.
The storm. Winds from the northwest at nearly hurricane force, and waves up to thirty-five feet.

The dark. Snow had closed in that afternoon. She had lost both of her radars. She was running for Whitefish Point almost blind, and when her captain asked about the radio beacon on the point, the one ships used to find their way in, he learned it wasn't working.
And the cold. Twenty-nine men went down with her, and not one of them was ever recovered. This time, the lake kept them all.
At ten past seven, her captain said, "We are holding our own." Minutes later, she was gone. Twenty-nine men. The same number of lives the Superior City lost in these waters, fifty-five years earlier.

If that just changed the way you see the Fitzgerald, do two things for me right now. Tap the like button, and if you haven't yet, subscribe. For a small channel like this one, that's the difference between this story reaching a few hundred people or a few hundred thousand.

sections.title: Her own hull
sections.dir: Measured and fair, like a careful reporter laying out evidence. Slow down for "was not seaworthy." The last paragraph is quiet and respectful.
paras: But there may have been a fourth killer that night. After our last Fitzgerald video, some of you who know these boats pointed me to it. The ship herself.

When she was built, she was designed to ride with a certain amount of her hull above the water. That's called freeboard. But in nineteen sixty-nine, nineteen seventy-one and nineteen seventy-three, the Coast Guard raised her load line, allowing her to carry heavier loads and ride more than three feet deeper than her original design. On her last night, her deck was only about eleven and a half feet above the water, in waves of up to thirty-five feet.

Her steward, who sailed on her for ten seasons and looked after her through seven winters, later testified that her keel was loose. He said parts of it were only tack welded, and that he had seen many of those welds broken. He was never asked to testify at the official inquiry.
And one of the engineers who helped design her hull later studied all of it, and concluded that on the tenth of November, nineteen seventy-five, the Edmund Fitzgerald was not seaworthy.

That's not the official answer. The Coast Guard blamed water coming in through her hatch covers. Others blame the waves alone, or a shoal she may have struck that day. And the wreck can't settle it. She lies in two pieces. Her bow stands upright in the mud. Her stern lies upside down, about a hundred and seventy feet away. Between them is a field of iron ore pellets and torn steel.

Her bell isn't down there anymore. In nineteen ninety-five, it was raised and taken to the museum at Whitefish Point. A replica was left in its place, engraved with the names of all twenty-nine men. Under Ontario law, no one can dive on her without a license. She's a grave.

sections.title: Let the water back
sections.dir: Gentle and reflective, slower. Pause between the things disappearing. The last paragraph is direct and friendly.
paras: Now let the water back in.

Lake Superior rises over the Fitzgerald first. Then the deep wrecks of the preserve. The Superior City disappears. Then the Comet, and whatever is left of her silver. The Cowle, the Vienna, the Niagara. The Myron and the Miztec slip under together. Then the Saturn's broken timbers, and the water is back at the foot of the lighthouse.

Tomorrow, freighters will pass Whitefish Point the way they have for more than a hundred and seventy years. Every one of them sails over this graveyard. And once you know the story, you never look at that water the same way again.

If you've sailed past Whitefish Point, worked on the boats, dived these wrecks, or visited the museum there, I'd really like to hear from you. Stories from people like you are the best part of this channel. Tell me yours in the comments.

sections.title: Your verdict
sections.dir: Fair and calm for the question, like a careful reporter. Then warm and direct for the last paragraph, like saying goodnight to a friend.
paras: So, what sank the Edmund Fitzgerald? The storm, the dark and the cold were all there that night, the same three that have been sinking ships off Whitefish Point for two hundred years. But was it the waves? The hatch covers? A shoal? Or a ship that was carrying more than she was built for?
Now you've heard all of it. Tell me in the comments what you think, and why. And if you guessed earlier, tell me if you've changed your mind. I read every one.

And if you've watched all the way to here, you're exactly who this channel is made for. So if you haven't subscribed yet, do it now, and tap the bell. Because there are more graveyards hidden in these lakes, and we're going to find them. Thanks for watching.
